title: The Edge Isn't in the Farm
subtitle: If top GMs were beating the market on prospect math, the prospect-level features would separate them from the bottom. They don't. Something else does — and the chart tells the story before the prose does.

sections.content:
The companion piece to this one — The $5M GM Gap — established that GM identity is a real predictor of per-trade dollar surplus. The natural follow-up question is the more useful one: *what about* the top GMs makes them top GMs? If the answer is "they evaluate prospects better," the prospect-side features in the model should light up when you stratify by GM tier. If it is something else, those features will stay dark.

It is something else.

sections.title: Per-GM correlation between mean dollar surplus and each feature (48 GMs, ≥40 trades)
sections.caption: Each bar is the Pearson correlation between a GM's mean career dollar surplus and that GM's mean value of the feature, across the 48 qualifying GMs. Top of chart = features where high-performing GMs systematically differ from low-performing GMs. Bottom of chart = no signal. Payroll lands at essentially zero. Prospect features sit below the org-level features.

sections.title: What the bar chart says
sections.content: The top of the chart is dominated by two clusters: big-league acquired player quality, and organizational infrastructure (alumni network, dev fit). The prospect features (max FV, avg FV, MiLB pitch quality, origin dev cluster) sit in the bottom half, with correlations indistinguishable from noise. Payroll sits at the very bottom — slightly negative. The GMs at the top of the leaderboard are not getting there by spending more.

The single strongest signal is acquired player quality at the major-league level — a constructed index from the V3 feature set that combines recent WAR, age-relative-to-peak, and contract value of the players coming back in the trade. Each GM has a career-mean value of this index across all their receiver-side trades. Across 48 GMs, the correlation between that mean and the GM's mean dollar surplus is r = 0.45. That is the clearest visual in the dataset.

sections.title: Per-GM mean surplus vs mean acquired player quality (each point is a GM, sized by trade count)
sections.caption: Each dot is one GM with 40+ trades. Higher and to the right is better. Beane, Preller, Stearns, Mozeliak anchor the high-surplus group. Coppolella, Minasian, Young anchor the low-surplus group. The line of fit (implied) runs from bottom-left to top-right — r = 0.447 across 48 GMs.

sections.content: The contrast becomes uncomfortable when you replace the x-axis with prospect grades. Maximum FanGraphs FV — the highest scout grade attached to any player in the acquisition — is the variable most closely associated in the public discourse with "winning a trade." The trade-grade industry runs on the FV. The same 48 GMs sorted by their career mean max-FV-received against their career mean dollar surplus tells a different story.

sections.title: Per-GM mean surplus vs mean max FanGraphs FV of acquired prospects
sections.x_label: Mean max FV of acquired prospects
sections.caption: Same axes as the previous chart on the y-side, but max FV (FanGraphs prospect grade) on the x-side. Correlation r = 0.178. Many of the highest-surplus GMs — Beane, Stearns, Mozeliak, Anthopoulos — sit at x = 0, meaning they essentially never acquired a graded prospect in trades. The signal that distinguishes them is on the big-league side, not here.

sections.title: FV grade coverage
sections.content: Many GMs sit at max_fv = 0 because most trades they made did not include a prospect with a published FanGraphs FV grade. The Board only covers a small fraction of the prospect universe, and the trades that include any graded player are a smaller still. This is itself a finding: the prospect-grading industry covers a thin slice of the actual trade market, and the GMs who win the trade leaderboard mostly operate outside that slice.

When you split the same 48 GMs into a top-12 and bottom-12 quartile by mean surplus and compute the gap on each feature category, the asymmetry becomes hard to miss. Big-league acquired-player quality and organizational infrastructure separate the two groups by margins that clear statistical detection. Prospect features do not move.

sections.title: Top 12 vs bottom 12 GMs — mean feature value (z-scored)
sections.caption: Each pair of bars shows the top-12 GM-tier mean (blue) vs the bottom-12 mean (orange), z-scored against the full 4,327-trade sample so every feature is on the same scale. Org-level features (alumni network, dev fit hitting) and big-league acquired player quality open wide gaps. The three prospect features sit on top of each other near zero. Payroll is the only feature where top GMs sit below bottom GMs.

sections.title: The actionable form of this finding
sections.content: If GM skill is what we mean when we talk about "winning trades," it lives in two places that show up in the data: the quality of the established big-league player a team takes back, and the quality of the development infrastructure that player walks into on arrival. It does not live in the prospect ledger, and it does not live in the payroll. A team trying to learn from the leaderboard should rebuild its trade-deck around those two questions and treat FV-driven valuations as a secondary input, not a primary one.

stats.label: r — prospect avg FV vs surplus

sections.content: The decomposition exposes the cliché in trade analysis: that smart teams beat the market by finding hidden gems in the lower minors. The decomposition cannot rule out *some* hidden-gem effect — the prospect features here are aggregates, and selection at the individual prospect level is below the resolution of this analysis. But it does rule out the cliché operating in aggregate. Across 5,300 trades and 48 different decision-making regimes, the prospect-side knobs do not turn. The big-league and organizational knobs do, hard.

methodology_note: Per-GM aggregates computed across receiver-side trade legs from 2010–2024 for GMs with ≥40 trades (n=48). Each GM's mean dollar surplus, mean feature value, and trade count are computed from the V3 model's combined feature/outcome matrix. Pearson correlations across GMs use one observation per GM (not per trade) to avoid double-counting volume. Top-12 vs bottom-12 grouped means use Welch's t-test for inference; significant differences listed in the article body. Acquired player quality is a constructed index combining recent WAR, age-relative-to-peak, and contract value of acquired players; the V3 model uses it directly. Max FV is from FanGraphs The Board, with missing GMs/trades coded as 0 (FV grade coverage is itself a finding).
